response.text:
Of what they had to expect, the Minister knew no more than his son. He thought on May 12 that he was going to a friendly Government and people, true to the anti-slavery principles which had been their steadiest profession. For a hundred years the chief effort of his family had aimed at bringing the Government of England into intelligent coöperation with the objects and interests of America. As for the private secretary himself, he was, like all Bostonians, instinctively English. He could not conceive the idea of a hostile England. He supposed himself, as one of a famous anti-slavery family, to be welcome everywhere in the British Islands.

On May 13, he met the official announcement that England recognized the belligerency of the Confederacy. This beginning of a new education tore up by the roots nearly all that was left of Harvard College and Germany. He had to learn—the sooner the better—that his ideas were the reverse of truth; that in May, 1861, no one in England—literally no one—doubted that Jefferson Davis had made or would make a nation, and nearly all were glad of it, though not often saying so. The sentiment of anti-slavery had disappeared. Lord John Russell had received the rebel emissaries and decided to recognize their belligerency before the Minister's arrival, in order to fix the British position in advance.

The first effect of this shock upon the son produced only a dullness of comprehension—a hazy inability to grasp the missile or realize the blow. Yet he realized that to his father it was likely to be fatal. When he thought over it in later life, he grew cold at the idea of his situation had his father then shown himself unfit for his post. That the private secretary was unfit for his—trifling though it were—was proved by his unreflecting confidence in his father. He passed this long day and tedious journey to London without once thinking of the possibility that his father might make a mistake. Whatever the Minister thought, his manner was the same as ever; his mind and temper as perfectly balanced; not a word escaped; not a nerve twitched.

The test was final, for no other shock so violent and sudden could possibly recur. The worst was in full sight. Dumped into Maurigy's Hotel at the foot of Regent Street, in the midst of a London season, without a friend or even an acquaintance, he preferred to laugh at his father's bewilderment before the waiter's "'amhandheggsir" for breakfast, rather than ask a question or express a doubt.

Politically and socially, the outlook was desperate. A newcomer in London society needs years to establish a position, and Minister Adams had not a week to spare. Yet Mr. Adams was always one of the luckiest of men, both in what he achieved and in what he escaped. Lord John Russell had probably acted kindly by him in forestalling his arrival; the blow must have fallen within three months and would then have broken him down. The British Ministers were a little ashamed of themselves, and certain to wait the longer for their next step in proportion to the haste of their first.

This is not a story of the diplomatic adventures of Charles Francis Adams, but of his son Henry's adventures in search of an education, which, if not taken too seriously, tended to humor. The father's position in London was not altogether bad; the son's was absurd. To him, the Legation was social ostracism, terrible beyond anything he had known. Entire solitude in the great society of London was doubly desperate because his duties required him to know everybody and go with his father and mother everywhere they needed escort.

He began to doubt whether secretaries were meant to be useful. Most secretaries detested their chiefs. At the St. James's Club, the most instructive conversation he ever heard among the young men of his own age was: "Quel chien de pays!" or, "Que tu es beau aujourd'hui, mon cher!" No one wanted to discuss affairs; still less to give or get information. Empires were always tumbling to pieces and diplomats were always picking them up.

His social education was more barren still. His little mistakes in etiquette made him writhe with torture. At one garden-party in Chiswick the Minister and Mrs. Adams were kept in conversation by an old anti-slavery Duchess Dowager till every one else went away except the young Duke and his cousins, who set to playing leap-frog on the lawn. At intervals during the next thirty years Henry Adams continued to happen upon the Duke, who, singularly enough, was always playing leap-frog.

When the end of the season came, the private secretary had not yet won a private acquaintance, and he hugged himself in his solitude when the story of Bull Run appeared in the *Times*. Bull Run was a worse diplomatic than military disaster. Yet the effect on the Legation was almost strengthening. They no longer felt doubt. For the next year they went on only from week to week, ready to leave England at once.

One December afternoon, in the solitude of Mansfield Street, Reuter's telegram announcing the seizure of Mason and Slidell from a British mail-steamer was brought to the office. All three secretaries—nervous as wild beasts under the long strain—knew it to be not merely diplomatic rupture but a declaration of war, and broke into shouts of delight. They were glad to face the end. Since England was waiting only for its own moment to strike, they were eager to strike first. At the moment of sharpest suspense, the Prince Consort sickened and died. Portland Place at Christmas in a black fog was never a rosy landscape, but in 1861 the most hardened Londoner lost his ruddiness.

He was mistaken—of course! He had been mistaken at every point of his education. The Trent Affair had one result personal to him that left no trace on the Legation records: it put an end forever to the idea of being "useful." He had been writing to the *New York Times* and to friendly London papers; he had even gone down to Manchester to study the cotton famine, and his account, printed with his name in the *Boston Courier*, came back upon him in the most crushing shape possible—a long, satirical leader in the London *Times*. Luckily the *Times* did not know its victim to be part of the Legation. He was totally unknown; London was empty; no one thought twice about it. Henry Adams escaped, but he never tried to be useful again. "Surtout point de zèle!" Zeal was too hazardous a profession for a Minister's son to pursue, as a volunteer manipulator, among Trent Affairs and rebel cruisers.

The Trent Affair passed like a snowstorm, leaving the Legation, to its surprise, still in place. The heavy months dragged on; winter slowly turned to spring without improving his position or spirits. His one social relief, during two years of miserable solitude, was the days he passed at Mount Felix as the guest of the Russell Sturgises—the single source of warmth and light in this social polar winter.

Very slowly, but quite steadily, the Minister and Mrs. Adams gained foothold. British society had begun with violent prejudice against Lincoln, Seward, and all Republican leaders except Sumner. Lord John Russell set the example: personally the Minister was to be kindly treated; politically he was negligible; he was there to be put aside. Every one waited to see Lincoln and his hirelings disappear in one vast *débâcle*.

This situation made Minister Adams an exception among diplomats. The Governments of Europe regarded the Washington Government as dead, and its Ministers as nullities. Minister Adams was better received than most nullities because he made no noise. Little by little, society took the habit of accepting him, not so much as a diplomat, but rather as a member of opposition, or an eminent counsel retained for a foreign Government. Barriers of race, language, birth, habit, ceased to exist. Earl Russell could not hold Mr. Adams apart. He was undistinguishable from a Londoner.

The singular luck that took him to Fryston to meet the shock of the Trent Affair under the sympathetic eyes of Monckton Milnes and William E. Forster never afterwards deserted him. Both saw the hopeless position they were in if the American Minister made a mistake, and lost no time in expressing to all the world their estimate of his character. Milnes was a social power in London, a maker of men; behind his Falstaffian mask he carried a fine, broad intelligence which no one questioned. Forster was his opposite: a tall, rough, ungainly Yorkshireman, kindly by inheritance from Quaker ancestry, who took up the Union cause as its practical champion in the House. With Bright and Cobden as further allies—the hardest hitters in England, classed as anarchists if hatred of the established orders made them so, strangers to London society but at home in the American Legation—the Minister could tackle even Lord Palmerston without much fear of foul play.

For the second time the British Ministry felt a little ashamed of itself after the Trent Affair, and disposed to wait before moving again. Friends gathered who were no fair-weather companions: the Duke of Argyll, the Duchess as true as her mother, the Trevelyans, the Lyells, Tom Hughes. Even the private secretary shared faintly in the social profit, and never forgot dining one night at the Lodge and finding himself engaged in instructing John Stuart Mill about the peculiar merits of an American protective system. By the time society began to reopen its doors after the death of the Prince Consort, even the private secretary occasionally saw a face he knew, although he made no more effort of any kind, but silently waited the end. Whatever might be the advantages of social relations to his father and mother, to him the whole business of diplomacy and society was futile. He meant to go home.
